title: Async Communication for Remote Teams
summary: A remote team runs on messages someone can act on half a day later. How to write the whole thought, record decisions, set reply tiers and leave a handoff that works.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The message lands at 10:43 p.m. for one teammate and 9:43 a.m. for the other: "Can you check this when you have a minute?" There's a link, a screenshot, and nothing else. No word on what changed, what decision is needed, or whether a release is waiting on it. The sender thinks they asked a small favor. The receiver now has a small mystery.

In an office, that message gets fixed in ten seconds. You lean over and ask "check what, exactly?" On a remote team across time zones, the same fix can take half a day, and the work sits still while the two of you take turns asking.

You don't need more meetings or longer documents. A handful of writing habits is enough to let the next person pick up the work without guessing. Basecamp, the company behind the project tool of the same name, publishes its internal communication rules, and the second one sums up the default: "Real-time sometimes, asynchronous most of the time" (How we communicate). Here's what makes the asynchronous part work.

Write the whole thought

A good async message reads less like a ping and more like a tiny handoff. Someone should be able to open it after lunch, get the state of things and decide on their own: act now, act later, or ask one sharper question.

The details you leave out are the ones that feel obvious to you, because you've been inside the problem all morning. The reader is coming in cold. A quick way to check is to answer the questions they'd ask if they could lean over to your desk:

What the reader wonders A line that answers it
What happened? "Payment webhook tests have failed on staging since 08:00."
Why should I care? "Release 4.2 can't go out until they pass."
What have you tried? "Yesterday's config change isn't it. I reverted it and the tests still fail."
What do you need from me? "Is the new retry header expected on your side?"
How urgent is it, really? "If we hear back before 15:00 your time, we ship today. Otherwise it moves to Monday, which is fine."

That's five short sentences. Writing them takes two minutes and saves a round trip that could cost a day. Basecamp puts the principle bluntly: "If it's important, critical, or fundamental, write it up, don't chat it down."

Write decisions down where people will look

Plenty of decisions get made on calls and survive only as somebody's memory. Two weeks later a new teammate asks why the team picked the simpler design or postponed an edge case, and nobody can quite say. The team either reopens the whole debate or trusts whoever sounds most confident.

Michael Nygard's 2011 post on architecture decision records names the problem well. Without the reasoning, a newcomer can only accept the decision blindly or reverse it blindly, and Nygard says it's better to avoid both. His format is short: a title, the context (the forces at play), the decision, its status, and the consequences. The whole thing should be one or two pages long.

Not every choice needs a formal ADR. A short note in the ticket or the team channel works for most: what we decided, why, what we turned down, and when we'd revisit it. What matters is that people can find it later. For more on that, see keeping meeting notes close to decisions.

Agree on how fast is fast enough

Remote teams often read silence as a bad sign, because nobody knows what a normal delay looks like. If every message might be urgent, people keep one eye on chat all day. If nothing is ever marked urgent, the real fire shows up late.

That always-on mode has a cost. In a lab study at CHI 2008, Gloria Mark and colleagues had people answer a stack of work emails while a "supervisor" interrupted them. When interrupted, people actually finished faster, with no drop in quality. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort (The Cost of Interrupted Work). People kept up by speeding up, and paid for it in strain.

Basecamp's guide calls the expectation of an immediate reply "toxic." The practical answer is to write down your response tiers, so nobody has to guess:

  • Incidents: page the on-call person. Expect a reply in minutes.
  • Same day: a direct mention in the team channel. Expect a reply before that person's day ends.
  • Everything else: a thread or a ticket. A reply within a working day is normal, and slower isn't rude.

Once those tiers exist, someone doing a careful review can close Slack for 90 minutes without feeling irresponsible. They know a real emergency will reach them another way.

Leave a map for the next person

Handoffs show how healthy a team's async habits are. A pile of links isn't a handoff. A good one is a small map: where things stand, the risks you know about, the questions still open, where the evidence lives, and what "done" looks like.

A handoff template

Status: what works, what doesn't. Risks: what might bite. Open questions: who could answer each one. Evidence: links to the logs, the PR, the dashboard. Done when: the check that tells us we're finished.

Time zones make this obvious, but it helps every team. People come back from a long meeting, a sick day, a week off or a morning of deep work, and they need a way back in that doesn't involve rebuilding the story from scattered messages.

Know when to just call

Async-first doesn't mean async-only. Some things go better live: a disagreement that's getting tense, sensitive feedback, mentoring, or a messy problem with so many moving parts that the thread keeps going in circles. A decent rule of thumb is that once a thread passes three rounds without converging, a 15-minute call is cheaper.

Basecamp calls meetings "the last resort, not the first option," and there's a reason. "Speaking only helps who's in the room, writing helps everyone." So when you do call, write the outcome back into the thread afterward, so the people who weren't there aren't left behind.

Try this week

  • Before you send your next "can you check this?", add the five lines from the table.
  • Write down your team's three response tiers and pin them in the main channel.
  • After your next decision call, post a five-line decision note before you close the laptop.
  • The half-day test: if a teammate went offline for half a day, could they come back and know what changed, what matters and what's expected of them? If not, start with the handoff template.

faqs.q: What should an async message include?
faqs.a: Enough for the reader to act without asking back: what happened, why it matters, what you already tried, exactly what you need from them, and how urgent it really is. Five short sentences usually cover it, and they save a round trip that can cost a full day across time zones.

faqs.q: How fast should people reply on a remote team?
faqs.a: Agree on tiers instead of one rule. Incidents go through paging and get a reply in minutes. Direct mentions get a reply the same working day. Threads and tickets can take up to a working day. Writing the tiers down lets people focus without worrying they'll miss a real emergency.

In a 2008 lab study by Gloria Mark and colleagues, people interrupted while answering emails finished faster with no loss in quality, but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. The work got done, and people paid for it in strain.

faqs.q: What is an architecture decision record?
faqs.a: A short document, one or two pages in Michael Nygard's original format, with a title, the context, the decision, its status and its consequences. It records why a choice was made, so later teammates neither accept it blindly nor reverse it blindly.

faqs.q: When should a remote team switch to a call?
faqs.a: When a disagreement is getting tense, when the feedback is sensitive, for mentoring, or when a thread keeps going in circles. After the call, write the outcome back into the thread so people who missed it can catch up.
